title: Xanthe and the Radiators
premise: Tamsin Oyelaran, a translator who has spent thirty years smoothing herself into other people's sentences, returns to her family's decaying house in Ibadan to clear it for sale and discovers a cache of undelivered letters hidden behind her grandmother's wardrobe — letters that reveal the family's founding silence: the child given away, the inheritance rerouted, the lie everyone agreed to keep. As she translates the letters from a dialect she is losing word by word, Tamsin realizes each relative has built an identity on a different version of the same story, and that exposing the truth will cost her the belonging she has never quite had. When the last letter names her own mother as the one who sealed the cache, Tamsin must choose between protecting the family's fragile peace and delivering, at last, what was written. In the end she reads the letters aloud at a family gathering, loses some of them forever, and gains — for the first time — a self spoken in her own words.
about_author: D. M. Quintana is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between Lagos and Manchester and writes about families that communicate exclusively through omission. Xanthe and the Radiators is their second novel, written in rooms where radiators clanked like impatient relatives.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In London, Tamsin translates a corporate report and deflects a colleague's question about home with her practiced smile. A call comes: her aunt Funmi has died, and the Ibadan house must be cleared within six weeks. Emotional beat: competent numbness masking dread of return.

chapters.title: Six Weeks and a Suitcase
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She packs, arguing by phone with her brother Seyi about selling versus keeping the house. Her mother, Adaeze, refuses to discuss the trip at all. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack — why won't Mother even say the house's name?

chapters.title: The House That Breathes
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Arrival in Ibadan; heat, geckos, the radiators her British-educated grandfather installed decades ago, absurd and beloved. Cousin Chidera greets her with warmth edged with warning: 'Some things you shouldn't move.' Emotional beat: homecoming as mild vertigo.

chapters.title: Inventory of Absences
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She begins cataloguing belongings, noticing which rooms were locked after Funmi's death and which portraits have been turned to face the wall. Seyi arrives, breezy and evasive. Emotional beat: the house as an archive of deliberate gaps.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Moving the wardrobe to patch a leaking roof, she finds a cavity holding forty-one letters, bundled and addressed but never sent — all in her grandmother Nnedi's hand, in Igbo mixed with a dying local dialect. Emotional beat: electric guilt and fascination.

chapters.title: Words I Used to Know
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with flashbacks. She begins translating the first letters, stumbling over vocabulary her tongue no longer holds; she calls a retired linguist, Professor Balogun, for help. The letters mention 'the arrangement.' Emotional beat: grief for a language slipping away mid-sentence.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Chidera's POV. Chidera, who cared for Funmi, reveals fragments: there was once another child, Nnedi's firstborn, sent away in 1968, and money that should have been his was quietly redirected. Emotional beat: complicity — Chidera knows more than she says and chose loyalty over truth.

chapters.title: Letters 1–9: A Boy Named Xanthe
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The early letters trace Nnedi's son Xanthe, fostered to a family in Enugu during the war, promised return that never came. Each letter asks a relative to fetch him; none were sent. Emotional beat: mounting horror at how many people failed to post them.

chapters.title: Seyi's Version
chapters.summary: Seyi's POV. Seyi privately admits he found one letter years ago and burned it, believing the truth would shatter Adaeze, whose entire authority rests on being Nnedi's heir. Emotional beat: protective corruption — love weaponized into concealment.

chapters.title: Adaeze's Silence
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Adaeze arrives at the house, sees the opened wardrobe cavity, and goes cold. She forbids Tamsin to continue, invoking family unity. Flashback hints: Adaeze met Xanthe once, as a girl, and said nothing. Emotional beat: fear wearing the mask of duty.

chapters.title: Professor Balogun's Parlor
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With Balogun, Tamsin translates the middle letters; the dialect unlocks memories of her grandmother's voice. One letter names the fostering family and includes an address in Enugu. Emotional beat: recovery — language returning as she chooses to look.

chapters.title: The Man Who Waited
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV (new). In Enugu, an elderly man — Xanthe himself, alive — keeps a shoebox of returned envelopes he mailed to Ibadan over fifty years, all marked undeliverable. He receives a researcher's call about estate records. Emotional beat: patient devastation, hope he no longer trusts.

chapters.title: Letters 10–27: The Money
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The later letters expose how Nnedi's brother funneled the inheritance meant for Xanthe into the family business that made everyone comfortable — including Tamsin's London salary, funded by a family trust. Emotional beat: complicity lands on her own skin.

chapters.title: Chidera's Bargain
chapters.summary: Chidera's POV. Chidera offers Tamsin a deal: burn the letters and Chidera will give her Nnedi's diary, which explains why Nnedi ultimately obeyed the family. Tamsin hesitates — the diary tempts her. Emotional beat: temptation of the curated truth.

chapters.title: What the Diary Says
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She accepts the diary and reads Nnedi's account: coerced during the war, threatened with losing all her children, Nnedi chose survival and spent her life writing letters she couldn't send. Emotional beat: compassion replacing judgment; the corruption of power shown from below.

chapters.title: Confrontation on the Landing
chapters.summary: Dual focus, Tamsin and Adaeze. Adaeze discovers the missing letters and the diary; mother and daughter collide on the staircase. Adaeze confesses she met Xanthe at fourteen and kept silent to protect her place as sole heir. Emotional beat: the family's architecture of lies exposed beam by beam.

chapters.title: Seyi Burns Nothing
chapters.summary: Seyi's POV. Seyi, expecting to repeat his old cover-up, instead finds Tamsin has already photographed every letter. Cornered, he breaks: he confesses the burned letter and his role in stalling the sale. Emotional beat: shame cracking into relief.

chapters.title: The Address in Enugu
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin travels to Enugu, finds Xanthe's modest compound, and stands at his gate unable to knock — until he opens the door, having recognized her name from the researcher's call. Emotional beat: terror and tenderness at the threshold.

chapters.title: Xanthe Speaks
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Over two days, Xanthe tells his story: the fostering, the returned letters, the life he built anyway — students, a garden, a quiet dignity. He does not want money; he wants to be read. Emotional beat: grace without absolution.

chapters.title: The Gathering
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin convenes the family in the Ibadan house and reads the letters aloud, all forty-one, refusing to soften or summarize. Relatives storm out, weep, deny; Adaeze sits unmoving until the final line. Emotional beat: climax — truth as an act that cannot be unsaid.

chapters.title: After the Reading
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs briefly. Fallout: the trust is dissolved, the house's sale redirected to fund Xanthe's scholarship fund; Adaeze, stripped of her story, begins — haltingly — to write her own account. Emotional beat: wreckage that is also open ground.

chapters.title: A Word Returned
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Months later, Tamsin visits Xanthe again, translating nothing for anyone but herself; she speaks to him in the old dialect, imperfectly, and he corrects her gently. She mails one letter of her own — to her future self. Emotional beat: belonging rebuilt not as inheritance but as choice.
